prompt: What does PostgreSQL start on the server for each client that connects?
hint: Look at the ps output after three psql sessions.

choices.text: A thread inside the postmaster
choices.why: PostgreSQL does not use threads for clients; ps showed separate processes.

choices.text: A whole operating-system process
choices.why: Right: `ana market [local] idle`, one per session.

choices.text: Nothing until the client sends its first query
choices.why: The three idle sessions had processes before sending anything.

choices.text: A slot in a shared queue served by the background writer
choices.why: The background writer writes pages; it does not serve clients.

prompt: `ps` shows each idle connection at about 13 MB of RSS. Why does that overstate what each one costs?

choices.text: RSS counts shared memory that every process touches
choices.why: Right: the private part, RssAnon, was about 3 MB.

choices.text: RSS is measured in pages of 8 kB, not in kilobytes
choices.why: ps reports RSS in kilobytes.

choices.text: The 13 MB is freed as soon as the session runs a query
choices.why: A query makes a process use more memory, not less.

choices.text: Idle sessions are swapped to disk
choices.why: The machine had no swap at all.

prompt: How many connections does the server allow with Ubuntu's default `max_connections`?
Why does `work_mem` make the memory of many busy connections hard to predict?
hint: It is not a per-server number.

choices.text: It is a total shared by all connections
choices.why: It is the opposite: each operation may take it.

choices.text: Each sort or hash gets up to it, per connection
choices.why: Right: and a complex plan holds several such operations at once.

choices.text: It only applies to superusers
choices.why: It applies to every session.

choices.text: It grows every time a connection is reused, until a restart
choices.why: It is a limit per operation, not a counter that grows.

prompt: In the curve, what happened to throughput between 4 and 90 clients?

choices.text: It grew in proportion to the clients
choices.why: Ninety clients did not do twenty times the work of four.

choices.text: It fell steadily as clients were added
choices.why: It stayed between 1334 and 1481; it did not fall steadily.

choices.text: It stayed about flat
choices.why: Right: four processors were busy from about four clients on.

choices.text: It doubled at each step
choices.why: Only from one client to four did it grow much.

prompt: With ninety clients and 1481 transactions a second, what average latency does Little's law give, in milliseconds?
hint: Clients in flight divided by throughput.

prompt: Why does the bend in the curve sit at about four clients on this machine?
hint: What did the machine have four of?

choices.text: Because pgbench uses four threads
choices.why: The threads only send the work; ninety clients were spread over them.

choices.text: Because max_connections divides into groups of four
choices.why: There is no such grouping.

choices.text: Because lesson 2's mix has four scripts
choices.why: It has six, and the scripts do not set how many run at once.

choices.text: Because it has four processors and the mix is mostly processor work
choices.why: Right: a mix that waits on the disk would bend later.

prompt: A team's database refuses connections at peak, with processors at 100%. They raise `max_connections` from 100 to 400. What does the curve predict?

choices.text: No more transactions a second, and each one slower
choices.why: Right: the errors stop and the waiting moves inside the server, at a higher cost.

choices.text: Four times the throughput
choices.why: The processors were already full; the limit was not what capped the work.

choices.text: The same latency as before, with more clients served
choices.why: Latency grew with every client added past the bend.

choices.text: A server that refuses to start
choices.why: It starts; the cost is paid in memory and contention while it runs.

prompt: With `default_pool_size = 8` and 200 clients, how many connections did the server see from PgBouncer?

choices.text: 200, one per client
choices.why: The server would have refused that; it is what direct connections tried.

choices.text: Eight
choices.why: Right: 192 clients waited in PgBouncer.

choices.text: 100, the server's maximum
choices.why: The pool size, not the server's limit, sets how many it opens.

choices.text: One, shared by all clients
choices.why: There were eight server connections active.

prompt: Why does the lesson point PgBouncer at the server through `host=127.0.0.1` rather than the Unix socket?
hint: PgBouncer runs as the postgres user.

choices.text: The socket is slower than TCP
choices.why: On one machine the socket is the faster of the two; speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Over the socket, peer authentication would log it in as postgres, not as ana
choices.why: Right: over TCP the server asks for the SCRAM proof PgBouncer can pass on.

choices.text: PgBouncer cannot open sockets
choices.why: It opens one itself, in unix_socket_dir.

choices.text: The server listens on 127.0.0.1 only
choices.why: It also listens on its socket; psql used it all along.

prompt: Through PgBouncer, 200 clients averaged 149 ms per transaction. Where was most of that time spent?

choices.text: Logging in to the server for every transaction
choices.why: The server connections stay open; that is the point of a pool.

choices.text: In TCP between pgbench and PgBouncer
choices.why: On one machine that is a fraction of a millisecond.

choices.text: Waiting in PgBouncer's queue
choices.why: Right: 192 were waiting, and a waiting client costs only a few kilobytes.

choices.text: Running each query eight times
choices.why: Each query runs once, on one of the eight connections.

prompt: Put the steps of the lesson's PgBouncer setup in order.
hint: The password has to exist before its secret can be copied.
items: Keep a copy of the original pgbouncer.ini and write the short one
Copy ana's SCRAM secret into userlist.txt
Restart pgbouncer and connect on port 6432
trap: Copying the secret before the password exists copies nothing, and restarting before the files are ready starts a pool nobody can log in to.

prompt: In `pool_mode = transaction`, when does a client give its server connection back?

choices.text: When it disconnects
choices.why: That is session mode.

choices.text: After every statement, even inside a transaction
choices.why: That is statement mode, which refuses multi-statement transactions.

choices.text: At the end of each transaction
choices.why: Right: at COMMIT or ROLLBACK, and a lone statement is its own transaction.

choices.text: When the pool is full and another client asks
choices.why: It gives it back at every transaction's end, whether anybody is waiting or not.

prompt: Session A ran `SET statement_timeout = '1s'` through a transaction pool. Later, Session B, which set nothing, showed `1s`. Why?

choices.text: PgBouncer copies settings to every client
choices.why: It copies nothing; if it did, Session A would have kept its own.

choices.text: B ran on the server connection A had set it on
choices.why: Right: process 8617 kept A's SET, and B was given it.

choices.text: The setting was made for the whole database
choices.why: SET changes one session; ALTER DATABASE would have been the whole database.

choices.text: statement_timeout defaults to one second through a pool
choices.why: Session A's first SHOW returned 0, the default.

prompt: Which of these break, or behave differently, through a transaction-mode pool? Choose all that apply.
hint: Anything that lives on the session.

choices.text: A session-level `SET`
choices.why: Right: it stays on the server connection, as Session A found.

choices.text: `pg_advisory_lock`
choices.why: Right: the lock stays on a connection the client no longer holds.

choices.text: `LISTEN`
choices.why: Right: between transactions the client has no connection to be notified on.

choices.text: `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction
choices.why: It ends with the transaction, on the same connection.

choices.text: A plain `SELECT` outside a transaction
choices.why: It is a transaction of its own and works as before.

prompt: In transaction mode, a client gives its server connection back to PgBouncer at `COMMIT` or at `___`.
hint: The other way a transaction ends.

prompt: The pool of eight gave 1342 tps in one run and 1235 in another. What does that do to the reading of 16 against 32 (1297 and 1353)?

choices.text: 32 is better by 56 tps, so it should be used
choices.why: 56 is less than the 107 the same setting varied by.

choices.text: The difference is inside the noise, so they cannot be told apart
choices.why: Right: and between two sizes that cannot be told apart, take the smaller.

choices.text: 16 is better, because latency matters more than throughput
choices.why: Latency was lower at 32 too, by less than the noise.

choices.text: The runs must be repeated with fewer clients
choices.why: The client count is fixed at 200 to compare pool sizes; the issue is noise.

prompt: Three application servers each run PgBouncer with `default_pool_size = 30` against one database with `max_connections = 100`. What is wrong?

choices.text: Nothing: each pool is under 100
choices.why: The server sees the sum of the three pools.

choices.text: PgBouncer refuses pool sizes above 20
choices.why: There is no such limit; the cost is on the server.

choices.text: 90 server connections leave little room for people, and sit far past the bend
choices.why: Right: migrations and incidents need room, and on four processors 90 busy connections only queue.

choices.text: Three poolers make the transactions run three times
choices.why: Each transaction runs once, through whichever pooler its client uses.

prompt: Match each number from PgBouncer's `SHOW POOLS` to what it tells you.
hint: The cl_ columns are clients, the sv_ columns are server connections.

pairs.right: clients queued for a server connection
how long the oldest waiting client has waited
when a connection is given back

right_distractors: how many clients the server refused

prompt: An application moved to a transaction-mode pool. Its reports start failing with `canceling statement due to statement timeout`, although the report code never sets a timeout. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Who else uses the same server connections?

choices.text: Another client's session-level `SET`, left on a shared connection
choices.why: Right: exactly what Session B received from Session A.

choices.text: PgBouncer cancels any statement longer than its pool timeout
choices.why: The message is the server's statement_timeout, which PgBouncer did not set.

choices.text: The pool is too small, so reports time out waiting
choices.why: Waiting in the pool does not raise this server error.

choices.text: Reports cannot run through a pool
choices.why: They run; what breaks is state left on the session.

prompt: Which statement does the lesson's measurement support?

choices.text: A pool made the server do more work than it could alone
choices.why: Throughput through the pool was about what ninety direct clients got.

choices.text: A pool let 200 clients in without refusals
choices.why: Right: the work done stayed about the same; the refusals disappeared.

choices.text: Raising max_connections to 200 would have matched the pool
choices.why: It would have run 200 processes past the bend, at a higher cost.

choices.text: Session mode would have served the 200 clients with eight connections
choices.why: Session mode needs one server connection per client.
